pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observation that HEA catalysts possess a broad, featureless valence band associated with diverse local electronic structures (PMC8163215::web::000 and PMC8163215::web::003).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a precisely controlled plasma-assisted nitrogen incorporation step tailored to subtly modify and protect the catalyst surface electronic structure—distinct from the synthesis route in the paper—aimed at mitigating deactivation under automotive exhaust conditions.

fields.hypothesis: Optimized low‐energy nitrogen plasma treatment to gently incorporate nitrogen into the catalyst surface, forming a sub‐nanometer nitride-rich layer that preserves the inherent electronic heterogeneity of the multi‐element alloy while mitigating deactivation.
fields.material_initial_state: A nearly equiatomic multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst with a uniform, metallic high-entropy surface showing a broad, featureless valence band.
fields.intervention: Expose the as-prepared catalyst to a carefully calibrated low-energy nitrogen plasma treatment designed to incorporate nitrogen atoms solely into the outermost atomic layers.
fields.conditions: Plasma treatment conducted in a controlled nitrogen atmosphere at low power (e.g., 30–50 W) and low substrate temperature (<200 °C) for a short duration (e.g., 1–2 minutes), followed by tests under transient low-temperature gasoline/hybrid exhaust conditions (with H2O and NO exposure) and accelerated thermal aging cycles.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultrathin, nitride-rich surface layer that maintains the random high-entropy atomic configuration beneath but subtly modifies the local electronic structure at the active sites.
fields.mechanism: The incorporated nitrogen slightly perturbs the metal d-electron distribution without blocking the active sites. This minor modification can decrease the susceptibility to overoxidation and poisoning by H2O/NO through the formation of robust metal–nitrogen bonds while preserving the desirable broad valence band characteristic reported in the HEA catalyst. In effect, the nitride layer serves both as a protective barrier and a fine-tuning agent of the adsorption energies for reactive intermediates.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, the nitrogen-plasma-treated catalyst should exhibit reduced overpotential shifts and slower degradation in turnover frequency during extended transient exhaust operation and thermal aging; activity loss should be measurably lower (though the precise improvement magnitude will need optimization).
fields.baseline: The original multi-element alloy catalyst that, while active, suffers from progressive activity loss and durability limitations under realistic exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The treatment must be optimized to form only a sub-nanometer nitride layer; excessive nitriding may block active sites or form an insulating phase. The intervention is envisioned to work best under mild plasma conditions.
fields.uncertainty: Precise plasma parameters need to be identified to guarantee nitrogen incorporation without altering the beneficial broad valence band structure, and long-term stability of the nitride layer under cycling conditions remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of catalysts: one undergoing the optimized low-energy nitrogen plasma treatment and one untreated. Use XPS/HAXPES to assess the depth and nature of nitrogen incorporation and confirm the preservation of the broad valence band. Then, subject both batches to accelerated thermal aging and simulated transient exhaust conditions (with controlled H2O and NO contents).
measurements: Electrochemical performance metrics (polarization curves, overpotential at fixed current density, turnover frequency) before and after aging.
Surface chemical state analysis via XPS/HAXPES to verify the formation of a nitride-rich layer and to monitor any changes in the valence band.
Durability metrics such as overpotential shift and % activity retention over cycling.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrogen plasma-treated catalysts either show no significant improvement in durability and activity retention relative to the untreated sample, or if surface analysis indicates the formation of deleterious nitride phases that block active sites, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The importance of stabilizing and tuning surface electronic properties for enhanced catalytic performance as demonstrated by the HEA catalyst’s broad valence band (PMC8163215::web::000 and PMC8163215::web::003), combined with known benefits of ceria coatings in mitigating oxidation and sintering.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies an ALD-based strategy to deposit an ultrathin ceria overcoat on a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst—a method not reported in the paper—to stabilize the active surface against deactivation while keeping platinum-group-metal consumption low.

fields.hypothesis: Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) of an ultrathin ceria overcoat to create a protective, self-limiting interfacial layer that stabilizes the multi-element catalyst surface while maintaining high activity at low platinum-group-metal loading.
fields.material_initial_state: A nearly equiatomic multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with homogeneous elemental distribution and an active, metallic surface displaying a broad electronic signature.
fields.intervention: Apply a single ALD cycle (or a few cycles optimized for sub-monolayer coverage) of ceria (CeO2) onto the catalyst surface.
fields.conditions: The ALD process should be performed at moderate temperatures (150–250 °C) using well-established precursors to deposit an ultrathin, conformal ceria layer (target thickness <1 nm). Following deposition, the catalyst is subjected to transient low-temperature gasoline/hybrid exhaust conditions with H2O and NO exposure, as well as accelerated thermal-aging protocols.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of a sub-monolayer ceria overcoat that partially interacts with the catalyst surface, preserving the underlying high-entropy structure while providing an oxygen-buffering interface that modifies local electronic states.
fields.mechanism: The ultrathin ceria layer acts as a protective barrier against aggressive species (such as H2O and NO) by virtue of its oxygen storage capacity, thereby mitigating oxidation and sintering. In addition, electronic interactions at the metal–ceria interface can modulate the d-band occupancy of surface metal atoms to fine-tune adsorption energies in a beneficial manner without impeding active site accessibility. This modification is designed to retard catalyst degradation while maintaining high catalytic turnover.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, the ALD ceria-coated catalyst should exhibit enhanced durability with lower overpotential increases and better activity retention during long-term exposure to transient exhaust conditions. The catalytic activity should remain at least comparable to the baseline if the ceria layer is sufficiently thin.
fields.baseline: The untreated multi-element alloy catalyst, which currently suffers from activity loss and durability issues under transient and aging conditions in low-temperature exhaust environments.
fields.boundary: The ceria overlayer must be kept ultrathin (sub-monolayer to <1 nm) to avoid significant blockage of active sites; overly thick coatings could hinder catalytic access and lower intrinsic activity.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal ALD parameters (number of cycles, growth temperature, precursor choice) for achieving a protective yet non-inhibitory ceria layer need to be determined, and the long-term stability of the metal–ceria interface under dynamic exhaust conditions is to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of catalysts: one sample coated with an ultrathin ceria layer by ALD and one uncoated control. Characterize surface morphology and overcoat thickness using TEM and XPS. Then, carry out accelerated aging tests under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions (with controlled H2O and NO atmospheres) and monitor electrochemical performance over cycling.
measurements: Electrochemical performance tests (polarization curves, overpotential measurements, TOF) before and after aging.
Surface analysis (TEM, XPS depth profiling) to verify the integrity and thickness of the ceria layer before and after aging.
Durability metrics such as overpotential shifts and activity retention percentages over multiple cycles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ceria-coated catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in durability and activity retention compared to the uncoated catalyst, or if surface analyses reveal degradation or excessive coverage of the ceria layer leading to blocked active sites, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: the finding from the paper that N-doping in high-entropy alloy catalysts forms multiple M–N bonds which synergistically enhance both activity and durability.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the N-doping strategy from fuel cell-oriented HEA electrocatalysts to multi-element automotive alloy catalysts operating in exhaust environments, addressing degradation mechanisms specific to transient and low-temperature gasoline/hybrid-vehicle operation.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled post‐synthesis ammonia treatment to induce interstitial nitrogen doping in the multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst will form robust metal–nitrogen (M–N) bonds and promote a Pt‐rich surface layer, thereby mitigating activity loss and improving durability under transient, low‐temperature, H2O/NO‐rich exhaust conditions.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic ratios of principal elements, including platinum-group metals concentrated in a core–shell-like structure or randomly alloyed.
fields.intervention: Perform a controlled post‐synthesis ammonia treatment (thermal treatment under NH3 atmosphere) at a temperature optimized below significant sintering limits to incorporate interstitial N atoms.
fields.conditions: Transient and low-temperature exhaust operation conditions typical for gasoline/hybrid vehicles; exposure to H2O and NO; and thermal aging/mileage effects.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of multiple M–N bonds that pin the surface atoms, promote a slight tensile strain in the Pt-rich surface, and suppress leaching/dissolution of transition metals.
fields.mechanism: N-doping creates strong chemical bonds (M–N) between the dopant N atoms and non-noble metal constituents, thereby stabilizing the alloy structure and modifying the surface electronic structure (i.e., tuning the d-band center) to weaken adsorption of poisoning species. The induced tensile strain in the Pt-rich layer facilitates optimal reactant binding and accelerates turnover, similar to the beneficial effects observed in N–Pt/HEA/C electrocatalysts (see PMC10859931 records).
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, this intervention is predicted to reduce activity decay (e.g., lower voltage loss and mass activity drop) by approximately 20–30% under extended cycling, with enhanced resistance to oxidation and metal dissolution.
fields.baseline: The untreated catalyst suffers from moderate metal dissolution and agglomeration, leading to activity loss and durability issues under operating exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The benefits are expected under the regime of transient, low-temperature (e.g., <350 °C) exhaust operation with exposure to H2O and NO and under conditions simulating long-term thermal aging.
fields.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in activity and durability may vary depending on the precise N content and treatment temperature; uncertainties remain in scaling lab-scale treatment to full automotive conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical multi-element alloy catalysts. Subject one set to the post‐synthesis ammonia treatment to induce N-doping and leave the other untreated. Expose both sets to simulated transient exhaust cycles with controlled H2O and NO levels and thermal aging protocols.
measurements: Catalyst mass activity (A mgPGM–1) over cycle number
Electrochemical surface area retention
Structural analysis (e.g., XRD, XAS) to check for M–N bond formation
Elemental leaching/dissolution assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ammonia-treated catalysts do not exhibit statistically significant improved activity retention or display similar/deteriorated structural degradation relative to the untreated catalysts, the hypothesis is invalidated.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: the understanding that interfacial oxide layers (such as those formed by N-doping in the paper) can stabilize catalyst structures, extended with the concept of oxygen storage and redox buffering provided by CeOx known in automotive catalyst systems.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a cerium-based intervention as a single modification to the multi-element catalyst, offering a novel strategy (distinct from N-doping or carbon coating) to buffer oxidative stresses and improve long-term durability in automotive exhaust conditions while still maintaining low platinum usage.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a low-level cerium (Ce) dopant during synthesis will promote the in situ formation of a Ce-oxide interfacial phase on the catalyst surface, which acts as an oxygen storage and release buffer, mitigating NO-induced oxidation and thermal degradation while preserving low platinum loadings.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic ratios and a partially segregated Pt-rich surface.
fields.intervention: Incorporate a small amount (e.g., <2 atomic %) of cerium precursor during the alloy synthesis, such that during subsequent processing (e.g., acid treatment and annealing) a thin CeOx interfacial layer is formed on or near the catalyst surface.
fields.conditions: Operation under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions with exposure to H2O and NO, and experiencing thermal aging or increased mileage that typically leads to catalyst degradation.
fields.structural_mediator: The CeOx phase forms at the interface with the alloy nanoparticles, acting as a protective buffer that can reversibly store and release oxygen, thereby modulating the local oxidative environment and protecting the catalyst surface from over-oxidation and metal leaching.
fields.mechanism: Cerium oxide is known for its oxygen storage capacity and redox properties. The thin CeOx interlayer can scavenge excess oxygen and NO during transient operations, reducing the direct oxidation of the active metal sites while maintaining an optimized electronic state for catalytic turnover. This mechanism not only protects against thermal degradation but also minimizes the loss of platinum-group metals. The intervention leverages well-known properties of ceria used in automotive exhaust catalysts (see TXT::wikipedia::Tungsten::020 for catalyst durability concepts and automotive applications).
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, the Ce-doped catalyst is expected to exhibit improved durability (e.g., lower Pt dissolution and reduced oxidation of transition metals) and stabilized catalytic activity, with potential activity retention improvements on the order of 15–25% over prolonged cycling.
fields.baseline: The untreated catalyst suffers from catalytic deactivation due to oxidative degradation, metal dissolution, and structural rearrangements induced by NO and H2O exposure during thermal aging.
fields.boundary: The CeOx interlayer must remain thin (to avoid blocking active sites) and effective primarily under the low-temperature, transient conditions; its protective effect may be limited at very high temperatures.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal cerium content and its distribution on the catalyst surface are open parameters; while the redox buffering action is well known, the magnitude of its impact in this specific multi-element alloy system is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two versions of the catalyst: one with a low-level cerium dopant and formation of the CeOx interface, and a control without cerium. Test both under simulated exhaust conditions with periodic exposures to H2O and NO and cycles of thermal aging.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of Pt and transition metal dissolution (ICP-MS)
Catalyst activity (mass activity, specific activity) tracking over cycles
Surface and interfacial characterization (XPS, TEM) to verify CeOx layer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the inclusion of cerium does not lead to a statistically significant improvement in durability or if the CeOx layer formation is absent or deleterious to catalytic performance, the hypothesis will be rejected.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The observed sacrificial oxidation and structural reversibility dynamics of non-noble metals in the HEA system (as discussed in PMC10466320::web::020) and principles of protective passivation known from corrosion literature.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a compositional modification of the HEA by incorporating a sacrificial element to deliberately create a self-passivating oxide layer during operation—a strategy not explored in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: Introduce a minor fraction of a sacrificial, highly oxidizable element into the HEA to form a self-passivating oxide layer during operation that protects active sites and improves durability under H2O/NO exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element HEA catalyst comprised of near-equiatomic elements (e.g., Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Pd) with known challenges of activity loss due to sintering and deactivation during prolonged exposure to exhaust gases.
fields.intervention: Alloy the catalyst with a small addition (approximately 2–5 atomic %) of a sacrificial metal such as manganese (Mn), which has a higher tendency to oxidize compared to the other constituents.
fields.conditions: Operated under transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions that include exposure to oxidizing species (H2O, NO) and subject to thermal aging from increased mileage.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a nanoscale, self-limiting passivating Mn-oxide layer selectively at the catalyst surface while leaving the underlying HEA clusters intact.
fields.mechanism: During exhaust operation, the sacrificial Mn preferentially oxidizes to form a protective, thin oxide overlayer. This passivating layer mitigates further oxidation and sintering of the active HEA sites, preserving their high activity and catalytic functionality. The coating is self-healing due to reversible redox reactions analogous to those observed for CeO2-supported HEA clusters.
fields.predicted_outcome: Enhanced durability and sustained catalytic activity (e.g., stable NO conversion at low temperatures) relative to the original HEA catalyst without sacrificial element addition; improved resistance to thermal aging and oxidative deactivation is expected, although the exact improvement magnitude remains uncertain.
fields.baseline: The untreated HEA catalyst that shows progressive deactivation under combined thermal and redox stress in low-temperature exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is contingent on maintaining a low substitution level; if the sacrificial element content is too high, it may dilute the active sites or block hydrogen spillover pathways.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of the sacrificial element for balancing protection and catalytic activity is uncertain and may require fine-tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two versions of the catalyst: one standard HEA and one with 2–5 at% Mn substituted in the alloy. Subject both to simulated low-temperature exhaust conditions containing H2O and NO, along with cyclic thermal aging. Monitor catalytic activity (NO conversion) and evaluate surface composition and oxide layer formation using XPS and TEM.
measurements: NO conversion vs. time and temperature
Surface oxide layer characterization (XPS, TEM)
Durability metrics over accelerated aging cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-alloyed catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in deactivation rate and/or improved catalytic activity compared to the standard HEA catalyst under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: the understanding that oxygen vacancies drive degradation in multi-component oxide systems (PMC12012691) and that targeted alloying can form passivation layers in high-temperature alloys (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::019).
pool.what_is_new: This approach strategically introduces a minor alloying element (Ti) to induce self-organized surface passivation during service, a concept not previously applied to multi-element automotive alloy catalysts aimed at low platinum consumption.

fields.hypothesis: Minor incorporation of titanium into the alloy can induce in-situ formation of a protective TiO2-rich passivation layer during aging, which will mitigate oxygen vacancy over-generation and suppress the degradation pathways associated with surface leaching.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic ratios containing transition metals that are prone to surface degradation via oxygen vacancy formation and subsequent leaching under exhaust conditions.
fields.intervention: Introduce a low concentration (approximately 1–2 atomic %) of titanium as a dopant during alloy synthesis.
fields.conditions: The catalyst is thermally cycled under conditions typical of transient, low-temperature exhaust operation with realistic exposures to H2O and NO.
fields.structural_mediator: Titanium, being a strong oxide former, segregates to the surface during thermal aging to yield a thin TiO2-rich passivation layer.
fields.mechanism: The formation of a TiO2 layer at the catalyst surface provides a thermodynamically stable barrier that limits the formation and migration of oxygen vacancies as well as the leaching of less stable 3d metals. This protective oxide reduces lattice strain and electronically stabilizes the active sites without hindering catalytic pathways, drawing on principles known from oxidation protection in superalloys (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::019).
fields.predicted_outcome: The Ti-doped catalyst is expected to show enhanced durability and more stable activity over extended thermal and mileage cycles, with lower degradation rates relative to the pristine alloy.
fields.baseline: The undoped catalyst suffers from uncontrolled oxygen vacancy generation leading to performance decline under thermal and exhaust-induced stresses.
fields.boundary: The Ti concentration must remain low; excessive Ti may dilute the active phase or form thick insulating TiO2 layers that decrease catalytic performance.
fields.uncertainty: The exact segregation behavior and protective layer thickness under operating conditions are uncertain, and performance gains may be modest.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two catalyst variants: one with 1–2 at% Ti and one without. Expose both to accelerated exhaust conditions with thermal cycling and H2O/NO exposure. Use XPS and TEM to analyze surface composition and layer formation, and track catalytic activity metrics (overpotential, activity loss) over time.
measurements: Surface Ti distribution and TiO2 layer thickness (via XPS/TEM)
Catalytic overpotential and activity retention over aging cycles
Comparative longevity testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped catalyst does not form a detectable TiO2-rich layer or does not exhibit improved durability and activity compared to the undoped catalyst, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C7
pool.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration of durable multi-active site electron transfer in HEA systems, extended by the introduction of in-situ formed nano-oxide dispersions as physical anchors to further combat degradation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a modification at the synthesis stage through the incorporation of a minor rare-earth (yttrium) addition—an approach not explored in the paper—to induce the formation of robust nano-oxide phases that enhance thermal and chemical durability under automotive exhaust conditions.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporate a minor addition of a rare-earth element (yttrium) during synthesis to promote the in-situ formation of finely dispersed Y₂O₃ nano-oxides on the catalyst surface, thereby enhancing thermal stability and reducing catalyst deactivation.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst comprised of nearly equiatomic principal elements and low platinum content, similar to the HEA nanoparticles characterized in the paper.
fields.intervention: Add a small amount (e.g., <1 atomic percent) of yttrium precursor to the synthesis mixture so that during nanoparticle formation, trace amounts of Y segregate and form highly dispersed Y₂O₃ nano-oxides on the surface.
fields.conditions: The catalyst is subsequently exposed to transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions, with the presence of H₂O and NO, and subjected to thermal aging and extended mileage.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a nano-oxide/metal composite structure where discrete Y₂O₃ particles are intimately dispersed on the HEA surface, acting as physical barriers against sintering and leaching.
fields.mechanism: Y₂O₃ is known for its high thermal stability and capability to inhibit particle coarsening. By incorporating yttrium into the precursor, minute Y₂O₃ nano-oxides will form in situ during synthesis and/or mild post-treatment. These oxides anchor the active metal nanoparticles and suppress deleterious metal migration or coalescence under harsh automotive exhaust conditions. Additionally, the nano-oxides can facilitate proper electron transfer by preserving the spacing and accessibility of multi-active sites, thus reducing activity loss caused by thermal aging.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Y-doped catalyst is expected to exhibit superior thermal stability and durability, with lower activity loss (potentially improved by tens of percent) relative to the pristine HEA catalyst, without increasing the platinum content.
fields.baseline: The untreated HEA catalyst, while initially active, shows progressive degradation due to sintering and non-selective leaching under prolonged exhaust exposure.
fields.boundary: The yttrium addition must be kept minimal; excessive doping may lead to extensive oxide formation that could cover active sites and hurt catalytic performance. The beneficial effect is anticipated only within a narrow composition range.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal yttrium concentration and the extent of in-situ Y₂O₃ formation require systematic optimization; precise quantitative improvement is uncertain until empirical data is obtained.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of catalysts: one including the minor yttrium addition in the precursor to induce Y₂O₃ formation, and one without yttrium. Expose both sets to accelerated aging tests under simulated exhaust conditions (with H₂O and NO and thermal cycling), and compare their performance and structural integrity.
measurements: Characterize nano-oxide formation using TEM and XPS to confirm the presence of well-dispersed Y₂O₃ particles on the catalyst surface.
Measure catalytic activity and durability (e.g., via current density or conversion efficiency) before and after aging tests.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: Findings from the paper that alterations in surface configuration can modify adsorption energy distributions (PMC7155130::web::005 and PMC7155130::web::012), combined with the known impact of controlled oxygen incorporation on the d-band electronic structure (KG::d_band_center::065121d0e0).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a plasma-based, single-step surface modification approach that specifically aims to fine-tune the AEDP and enhance durability under automotive exhaust conditions—a strategy not explored in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: A low-power, short-duration oxygen plasma surface treatment selectively modifies the catalyst surface to fine-tune the adsorption energy distribution while concurrently cleaning and passivating the surface against aggressive exhaust species.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with a nearly equiatomic, as-deposited CSS structure possessing an unmodified surface with inherent AEDP broadness.
fields.intervention: Expose the catalyst to a mild oxygen plasma (with controlled plasma power and short exposure time) under low-pressure conditions to subtly oxidize and clean the surface without altering the bulk CSS structure.
fields.conditions: Simulated transient, low–temperature exhaust operation conditions featuring cyclic exposure to H2O and NO and thermal aging representative of increased mileage in gasoline or hybrid vehicles.
fields.structural_mediator: A thin, uniformly modified surface layer with slight oxygen incorporation that slightly shifts the d-band center of surface atoms, thereby optimizing the peak position of the AEDP without significantly impeding the number of active sites.
fields.mechanism: The plasma treatment effectively removes adsorbed contaminants and can introduce a controlled degree of oxidation that alters the local electronic structure. This shift in the d-band center fine-tunes the binding energy distribution of active sites to align closer with the optimal adsorption energy. Simultaneously, the cleaner and partially passivated surface shows enhanced resistance to deactivation by H2O and NO under transient conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, the plasma-treated catalyst is expected to exhibit a measurable decrease in overpotential (indicative of a better-aligned AEDP) and improved durability under cyclic, low–temperature exhaust conditions. The improvement is expected to be moderate while preserving low platinum-group-metal consumption.
fields.baseline: The as-deposited catalyst which experiences gradual activity loss and surface degradation during prolonged exposure to exhaust gases and thermal cycling.
fields.boundary: The plasma exposure parameters (power, duration, oxygen partial pressure) must be carefully tuned to avoid excessive oxidation that might deteriorate the CSS or block active sites.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in catalytic performance and durability due to plasma treatment is uncertain, though the qualitative effect of tuning the surface electronic structure is supported by related studies (KG::d_band_center::065121d0e0).

Surface characterization (XPS, EELS) to assess oxygen incorporation and verify retention of the overall CSS integrity
Durability tests including accelerated aging protocols
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the plasma-treated catalysts do not demonstrate a significant shift in activity curves toward lower overpotentials or show evidence of detrimental over-oxidation (e.g., loss of CSS characteristics), then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration of the benefits of N-coordination in stabilizing isolated metal sites in high-loading SAC systems (PMC11227521::web::009, PMC11227521::web::010).
pool.what_is_new: This approach introduces a precisely controlled ALD process to deposit an ultrathin, porous, N-doped carbon overlayer on a multi-element alloy catalyst, a strategy not explored in the paper, aimed specifically at achieving simultaneous protection and maintained accessibility of active sites during automotive exhaust operation.

fields.hypothesis: Apply a controlled atomic layer deposition (ALD) of an ultrathin, porous N-doped carbon overlayer onto the alloy catalyst post-negative pressure annealing to stabilize atomically dispersed PGE sites while preserving reactant access and catalytic activity.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst that has been subjected to negative pressure annealing (with or without prior nitrogen pre-functionalization) to achieve atomic dispersion of PGEs, but which remains vulnerable to sintering or deactivation over time in exhaust environments.
fields.intervention: Immediately after the vacuum annealing step, deposit an ultrathin (approximately 1–2 nm) layer of N-doped carbon using ALD with parameters tuned for highly porous, conformal coatings.
fields.conditions: The ALD process is executed at moderate temperatures (e.g., 300–400 °C) under controlled precursor dosing to ensure precise thickness and porosity; following deposition, the catalyst is exposed to transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions with H2O, NO and subjected to thermal aging cycles.
fields.structural_mediator: Atomically dispersed PGE sites encapsulated under a conformal, ultrathin, porous N-doped carbon overlayer that both anchors and protects the active sites against sintering and degradation.
fields.mechanism: The precisely controlled ALD-deposited N-doped carbon layer binds to the already dispersed PGE atoms, similar to the stabilizing effect of N-coordinated supports shown in the paper (PMC11227521::web::010). The ultrathin, porous nature of the coating minimizes mass transfer limitations while serving as a barrier against sintering, moisture, and NO-induced deactivation, thereby enhancing both the activity and durability.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the catalyst without the overlayer, the ALD-coated catalyst should exhibit improved durability (lower activity loss upon thermal cycling) and sustained catalytic activity during transient exhaust operation, with minimal additional diffusion resistance. The expected improvement is qualitative and may be moderate, but the protective effect should be evident.
fields.baseline: Catalyst processed solely by vacuum annealing without any post-treatment coating, which is prone to further aggregation or deactivation under harsh exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The overlayer must remain ultrathin and porous; if the deposition conditions yield a thicker or less permeable coating, it may hinder reactant diffusion and reduce catalytic activity.
fields.uncertainty: Although N-doped carbon layers are known to stabilize isolated metal sites, the optimal ALD parameters (thickness, porosity) for balancing protection with catalytic activity in this complex alloy system remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set receives the ALD-deposited ultrathin N-doped carbon overlayer immediately after negative pressure annealing, and the other set remains uncoated. Subject both sets to simulated transient exhaust conditions with repeated thermal cycles, H2O and NO exposure.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional characterization (XPS, TEM, STEM) to verify coating thickness and preservation of isolated PGE sites.
Catalytic activity tests (TOF, conversion rates) under standardized exhaust simulations.
Durability testing over multiple cycles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated catalyst does not display significant improvements in maintaining atomically dispersed active sites and exhibits no measurable enhancement in catalytic performance and durability compared to the uncoated control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10

pool.what_is_new: Proposes a novel post-synthetic plasma intervention to deliberately induce an amorphous surface layer on a multi-element automotive catalyst, a strategy that differs from traditional thermal treatments and has not been addressed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A post-synthetic low-temperature plasma treatment that induces controlled surface amorphization will create an amorphous shell on the nearly equiatomic multi‐element catalyst, thereby reducing catalyst sintering and enhancing resistance to deactivation by H2O and NO during transient, low-temperature exhaust operation.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic composition synthesized as a solid-solution HEA nanocrystal.
fields.intervention: Apply a low-temperature plasma treatment (using an oxygen-deficient or inert plasma) to the as-synthesized catalyst to induce partial amorphization at the nanoparticle surface without compromising the bulk crystalline core.
fields.conditions: Conduct the plasma treatment at low temperatures (well below 200°C) in a controlled environment (using a suitable gas mixture such as Ar or a low oxygen/Ar blend) to ensure that only the outer few atomic layers become amorphous.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultrathin amorphous surface layer over the crystalline core, which acts as a barrier to atomic diffusion and sintering.
fields.mechanism: The plasma treatment disrupts the local crystalline order at the catalyst surface, generating an amorphous shell that can inhibit surface diffusion, reduce coalescence under thermal cycling, and prevent aggressive adsorption or poisoning by H2O and NO. The amorphous region may also provide a more uniform electronic environment for reactant adsorption, thus enhancing catalytic performance and durability.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared with an untreated catalyst, the plasma-treated catalyst is expected to exhibit significantly reduced sintering and improved durability under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions with water and NO exposure, while retaining comparable catalytic activity. The effect size is moderately predictable though exact quantitative improvements remain uncertain.
fields.baseline: Untreated multi-element catalyst that possesses fully crystalline surfaces that are more prone to sintering and degradation during thermal aging in automotive exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The plasma treatment must be optimized to avoid excessive amorphization that could block active sites or disrupt beneficial alloying. Its effectiveness is constrained by treatment uniformity and scale; benefits are expected primarily at the nanoparticle level.
fields.uncertainty: The extent of improvement in durability and resistance to deactivation is not precisely quantifiable without empirical data, and there is uncertainty regarding the optimal plasma parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst samples from the same synthesis batch. measurements: Surface structure analysis via high-resolution TEM and XPS to verify amorphous shell formation.
Catalytic activity and durability measurements over repeated thermal cycles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the plasma-treated catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in thermal stability and catalytic durability relative to the untreated sample—or if the plasma process degrades the catalyst’s activity—the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observations that a 500 °C/1.5-hour treatment fosters CSRO formation (PMC11809438::web::017::tem_characterization) combined with established metallurgical principles where defects enhance atomic diffusion and ordering (TXT::wikipedia::Tempering_(metallurgy)::002).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a two-step, single-intervention approach that integrates controlled mechanical attrition with a full 1.5-hour annealing treatment to deliberately induce CSRO at dislocation-rich surface regions—a novel variation from the standard furnace-aging method discussed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Controlled Surface Mechanical Attrition Followed by a 1.5-Hour Annealing Treatment to Promote Defect-Enhanced CSRO Formation.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with a homogeneous, nearly equiatomic solid solution surface that is vulnerable to sintering and catalytic degradation under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions (exposure to H2O and NO) and thermal aging.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled mechanical attrition process (such as optimized shot peening or laser shock peening) to the catalyst surface to induce a high density of surface dislocations and nanocrystalline regions, immediately followed by an annealing treatment at 500 °C for 1.5 hours in an inert Argon atmosphere.
fields.conditions: The mechanical attrition is performed under parameters that create a uniform, defect-rich nanostructured surface without causing macroscopic damage. Subsequently, the 500 °C anneal is conducted for 1.5 hours to enable sufficient atomic diffusion and ordering at the defect sites.
fields.structural_mediator: A surface substantially modified by a high density of dislocations and nanograins that, during the extended anneal, evolve into CSRO-enriched regions along grain and dislocation boundaries.
fields.mechanism: The induced high density of defects (dislocations, grain boundaries) accelerates localized diffusion during the annealing process, thereby providing preferential sites for CSRO formation. The well-developed CSRO at these defect sites reduces further atomic migration and sintering, effectively stabilizing the catalyst surface under transient operating conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated catalyst is expected to demonstrate significantly reduced surface sintering and improved durability under low-temperature, transient exhaust conditions compared to an untreated material. Enhanced catalytic activity retention should correlate with the extent of defect-mediated CSRO formation, with improvement on the order of that seen in conventional 500 °C/1.5-hour aging.
fields.baseline: An untreated catalyst that suffers from extensive sintering and degradation of catalytic performance under transient exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: Mechanical attrition conditions must be optimized to induce defects without causing excessive damage or initiating uncontrolled recrystallization. The 1.5-hour anneal must be sufficiently long to allow defect-assisted ordering without triggering unwanted grain growth in the bulk.
fields.uncertainty: While defect-enhanced diffusion is an established concept, the ability of a combined mechanical attrition and 1.5-hour anneal to consistently produce a beneficial CSRO network at the surface (without incurring detrimental recovery or recrystallization) remains to be fully demonstrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Take samples from a single catalyst batch and split them into two groups. Subject one group to controlled mechanical attrition (e.g., using shot peening) followed by a 1.5-hour anneal at 500 °C in Argon; leave the other group untreated. Characterize both groups with TEM and XRD to quantify dislocation density, grain size, and the presence of CSRO at the surface. Then, evaluate catalytic performance and sintering behavior under accelerated transient exhaust conditions (including exposure to H2O and NO).
measurements: TEM and XRD for quantifying dislocation density, nanocrystalline regions, and CSRO formation
Catalytic conversion efficiency and durability metrics under simulated exhaust conditions
Surface sintering evaluation via post-test electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically treated and annealed catalyst does not show a significant increase in defect-mediated CSRO formation or improved catalytic durability and reduced sintering compared to the untreated control, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: The paper's findings that forming a noble metal–rich surface (core–shell structure) increases stability through elevated dissolution potentials, but here the intervention uses cyclic redox conditions rather than post-synthetic galvanic replacement.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a cyclic oxidation-reduction pretreatment tailored for automotive exhaust conditions to promote in-situ, selective surface reordering—an approach not proposed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Implement a cyclic oxidation‐reduction pretreatment on the as‐synthesized equiatomic HEA catalyst to form a self-passivating, noble metal–enriched surface layer.
fields.material_initial_state: A nearly equiatomic, multi-element automotive alloy catalyst nanoparticle with a random distribution of platinum‐group and non‐noble metals.
fields.intervention: Expose the catalyst to a short-duration cyclic pretreatment where, first, the catalyst is heated in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., diluted O2 with H2O at 250–300 °C) for a brief period to preferentially oxidize the less noble, undercoordinated surface atoms, followed by a rapid switch to a reducing atmosphere (e.g., H2 or a hydrocarbon mixture) to reduce the oxidized species back to the metallic state.
fields.conditions: Pretreatment temperatures and durations low enough to avoid bulk grain growth yet sufficient for surface oxidation; subsequent catalytic operation under transient, low-temperature gasoline/hybrid exhaust conditions (with H2O and NO exposure and cycles of thermal aging).
fields.structural_mediator: A restructured nanoparticle surface in which the less stable non-noble metal sites are partially removed or reorganized, leading to enrichment of the more noble group metals (e.g., Pt or Au) on the (111) facets, thereby forming a protective, core–shell-like passivation layer.
fields.mechanism: Mild oxidation selectively targets the more reactive, low-coordination sites on the catalyst surface, oxidizing less noble elements that are prone to dissolution. During the rapid reduction step, the more noble elements remain in the metallic state and redeposit preferentially at the exposed high-coordination (111) sites. This controlled redox cycling mimics a self-passivation process similar to the core–shell structures reported in the paper, but here the driving force is the selective oxidation of vulnerable sites under exhaust-like conditions. This reorganization increases the local dissolution potentials of active sites, mitigating subsequent degradation during operation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated catalyst, the pretreated catalyst should show enhanced durability with a slower rate of surface atom loss and a retention of active (111) facets. The catalytic activity should be maintained or improved with minimal additional precious metal consumption since only a thin passivating skin is created.
fields.baseline: Untreated multi-element HEA catalysts that progressively lose active surface area due to non-selective dissolution under transient exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The pretreatment must be controlled such that only the surface undergoes oxidation/reduction without inducing bulk compositional shifts or sintering. It is applicable when the pretreatment atmosphere can be precisely switched and when the thermal budget is below that causing bulk diffusion.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative gains (e.g., % reduction in dissolution rate) are uncertain because the kinetics of selective oxidation and reduction in the simulated exhaust environment are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA catalyst nanoparticles. Subject one set to the described cyclic oxidation-reduction pretreatment and leave the other set untreated. Then, expose both sets to simulated low-temperature, transient exhaust conditions containing H2O and NO along with thermal aging cycles. Characterize the surface composition and morphology (using high-resolution TEM and XPS) and monitor dissolution rates via ICP spectroscopy, along with catalytic activity (e.g., turnover frequency or ECSA measurements) over time.
measurements: Surface elemental composition and mapping (TEM-EDS, XPS)
Dissolution rate of non-noble and noble metals (ICP spectroscopy)
Catalytic performance retention over time (ECSA, reaction rates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pretreated catalyst does not develop a statistically significant noble metal–rich, passivated surface layer and shows similar or accelerated dissolution and/or activity loss compared to the untreated catalyst, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.builds_on: While the paper focused on dissolution-driven surface reordering, this hypothesis builds on the general principle of protecting vulnerable surfaces from corrosive environments. fields.hypothesis: Apply a low-temperature atomic layer deposition (ALD) process to deposit an ultrathin, conformal alumina (Al₂O₃) overcoat on the HEA catalyst nanoparticles, thereby protecting the active surface from corrosive exhaust species while preserving catalytic sites.
fields.material_initial_state: A nearly equiatomic multi-element automotive HEA catalyst containing low amounts of platinum-group metals, with a randomly distributed surface composition.
fields.intervention: Utilize ALD to deposit a sub-nanometer (approximately 0.5–1 nm) layer of alumina over the catalyst. The ALD process is performed at low temperatures (e.g., below 150 °C) to avoid altering the bulk nanoparticle structure, ensuring that the coating is sufficiently porous or defect-rich to allow substrate access while acting as a protective barrier.
fields.conditions: The ALD process must be optimized to achieve a uniform, ultrathin overcoat and then the coated catalyst is subjected to transient, low-temperature automotive exhaust conditions (with H2O and NO exposures) and accelerated thermal aging cycles.
fields.structural_mediator: A conformal, self-healing alumina layer that physically inhibits corrosive agents from reaching and dissolving the underlying active metal surface while still allowing reactant (gas) diffusion to the active sites.
fields.mechanism: The ultrathin ALD alumina acts as a robust physical barrier that suppresses the ingress of H₂O, NO, and other corrosive constituents at low temperatures. Given the nanoscale thickness, the overcoat does not severely impede mass transport for catalytic reactions but limits the dissolution of vulnerable low-coordination sites. Under transient thermal conditions, minor defects in the overcoat may partially self-heal, maintaining an overall protective effect. This strategy is analogous to protective coatings used in thermal barrier applications (as described in the automotive exhaust context in background sources) but is now applied at the nanoscale for catalyst stabilization.
fields.predicted_outcome: The ALD-coated catalyst is expected to show significantly reduced rates of surface dissolution and improved durability under exhaust conditions when compared to the uncoated HEA catalyst, with maintained catalytic activity and low platinum-group metal consumption due to the ultrathin nature of the overcoat.
fields.baseline: Standard HEA catalysts without any protective overcoat, which suffer from progressive surface atom loss, dissolution, and activity degradation during exposure to automotive exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The ALD overcoat must be sufficiently thin (<1 nm) and porous enough to permit catalytic reactions while providing chemical stability. This method is applicable only if the ALD conditions do not cause sintering or alter the nanoparticle morphology.
fields.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the balance between protection and catalytic accessibility; if the overcoat is too thick or too impermeable, it may block active sites, while too thin a layer might not confer adequate protection. Quantitative improvements in durability need experimental calibration.

top3.label: C2
top3.builds_on: The importance of stabilizing and tuning surface electronic properties for enhanced catalytic performance as demonstrated by the HEA catalyst’s broad valence band (PMC8163215::web::000 and PMC8163215::web::003), combined with known benefits of ceria coatings in mitigating oxidation and sintering.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies an ALD-based strategy to deposit an ultrathin ceria overcoat on a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst—a method not reported in the paper—to stabilize the active surface against deactivation while keeping platinum-group-metal consumption low.

fields.hypothesis: Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) of an ultrathin ceria overcoat to create a protective, self-limiting interfacial layer that stabilizes the multi-element catalyst surface while maintaining high activity at low platinum-group-metal loading.
fields.material_initial_state: A nearly equiatomic multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with homogeneous elemental distribution and an active, metallic surface displaying a broad electronic signature.
fields.intervention: Apply a single ALD cycle (or a few cycles optimized for sub-monolayer coverage) of ceria (CeO2) onto the catalyst surface.
fields.conditions: The ALD process should be performed at moderate temperatures (150–250 °C) using well-established precursors to deposit an ultrathin, conformal ceria layer (target thickness <1 nm). Following deposition, the catalyst is subjected to transient low-temperature gasoline/hybrid exhaust conditions with H2O and NO exposure, as well as accelerated thermal-aging protocols.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of a sub-monolayer ceria overcoat that partially interacts with the catalyst surface, preserving the underlying high-entropy structure while providing an oxygen-buffering interface that modifies local electronic states.
fields.mechanism: The ultrathin ceria layer acts as a protective barrier against aggressive species (such as H2O and NO) by virtue of its oxygen storage capacity, thereby mitigating oxidation and sintering. In addition, electronic interactions at the metal–ceria interface can modulate the d-band occupancy of surface metal atoms to fine-tune adsorption energies in a beneficial manner without impeding active site accessibility. This modification is designed to retard catalyst degradation while maintaining high catalytic turnover.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, the ALD ceria-coated catalyst should exhibit enhanced durability with lower overpotential increases and better activity retention during long-term exposure to transient exhaust conditions. The catalytic activity should remain at least comparable to the baseline if the ceria layer is sufficiently thin.
fields.baseline: The untreated multi-element alloy catalyst, which currently suffers from activity loss and durability issues under transient and aging conditions in low-temperature exhaust environments.
fields.boundary: The ceria overlayer must be kept ultrathin (sub-monolayer to <1 nm) to avoid significant blockage of active sites; overly thick coatings could hinder catalytic access and lower intrinsic activity.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal ALD parameters (number of cycles, growth temperature, precursor choice) for achieving a protective yet non-inhibitory ceria layer need to be determined, and the long-term stability of the metal–ceria interface under dynamic exhaust conditions is to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of catalysts: one sample coated with an ultrathin ceria layer by ALD and one uncoated control. Characterize surface morphology and overcoat thickness using TEM and XPS. Then, carry out accelerated aging tests under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions (with controlled H2O and NO atmospheres) and monitor electrochemical performance over cycling.
measurements: Electrochemical performance tests (polarization curves, overpotential measurements, TOF) before and after aging.
Surface analysis (TEM, XPS depth profiling) to verify the integrity and thickness of the ceria layer before and after aging.
Durability metrics such as overpotential shifts and activity retention percentages over multiple cycles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ceria-coated catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in durability and activity retention compared to the uncoated catalyst, or if surface analyses reveal degradation or excessive coverage of the ceria layer leading to blocked active sites, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C12
top3.builds_on: The paper's findings that forming a noble metal–rich surface (core–shell structure) increases stability through elevated dissolution potentials, but here the intervention uses cyclic redox conditions rather than post-synthetic galvanic replacement.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a cyclic oxidation-reduction pretreatment tailored for automotive exhaust conditions to promote in-situ, selective surface reordering—an approach not proposed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Implement a cyclic oxidation‐reduction pretreatment on the as‐synthesized equiatomic HEA catalyst to form a self-passivating, noble metal–enriched surface layer.
fields.material_initial_state: A nearly equiatomic, multi-element automotive alloy catalyst nanoparticle with a random distribution of platinum‐group and non‐noble metals.
fields.intervention: Expose the catalyst to a short-duration cyclic pretreatment where, first, the catalyst is heated in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., diluted O2 with H2O at 250–300 °C) for a brief period to preferentially oxidize the less noble, undercoordinated surface atoms, followed by a rapid switch to a reducing atmosphere (e.g., H2 or a hydrocarbon mixture) to reduce the oxidized species back to the metallic state.
fields.conditions: Pretreatment temperatures and durations low enough to avoid bulk grain growth yet sufficient for surface oxidation; subsequent catalytic operation under transient, low-temperature gasoline/hybrid exhaust conditions (with H2O and NO exposure and cycles of thermal aging).
fields.structural_mediator: A restructured nanoparticle surface in which the less stable non-noble metal sites are partially removed or reorganized, leading to enrichment of the more noble group metals (e.g., Pt or Au) on the (111) facets, thereby forming a protective, core–shell-like passivation layer.
fields.mechanism: Mild oxidation selectively targets the more reactive, low-coordination sites on the catalyst surface, oxidizing less noble elements that are prone to dissolution. During the rapid reduction step, the more noble elements remain in the metallic state and redeposit preferentially at the exposed high-coordination (111) sites. This controlled redox cycling mimics a self-passivation process similar to the core–shell structures reported in the paper, but here the driving force is the selective oxidation of vulnerable sites under exhaust-like conditions. This reorganization increases the local dissolution potentials of active sites, mitigating subsequent degradation during operation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated catalyst, the pretreated catalyst should show enhanced durability with a slower rate of surface atom loss and a retention of active (111) facets. The catalytic activity should be maintained or improved with minimal additional precious metal consumption since only a thin passivating skin is created.
fields.baseline: Untreated multi-element HEA catalysts that progressively lose active surface area due to non-selective dissolution under transient exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The pretreatment must be controlled such that only the surface undergoes oxidation/reduction without inducing bulk compositional shifts or sintering. It is applicable when the pretreatment atmosphere can be precisely switched and when the thermal budget is below that causing bulk diffusion.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative gains (e.g., % reduction in dissolution rate) are uncertain because the kinetics of selective oxidation and reduction in the simulated exhaust environment are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA catalyst nanoparticles. Subject one set to the described cyclic oxidation-reduction pretreatment and leave the other set untreated. Then, expose both sets to simulated low-temperature, transient exhaust conditions containing H2O and NO along with thermal aging cycles. Characterize the surface composition and morphology (using high-resolution TEM and XPS) and monitor dissolution rates via ICP spectroscopy, along with catalytic activity (e.g., turnover frequency or ECSA measurements) over time.
measurements: Surface elemental composition and mapping (TEM-EDS, XPS)
Dissolution rate of non-noble and noble metals (ICP spectroscopy)
Catalytic performance retention over time (ECSA, reaction rates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pretreated catalyst does not develop a statistically significant noble metal–rich, passivated surface layer and shows similar or accelerated dissolution and/or activity loss compared to the untreated catalyst, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C3
top3.builds_on: the finding from the paper that N-doping in high-entropy alloy catalysts forms multiple M–N bonds which synergistically enhance both activity and durability.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the N-doping strategy from fuel cell-oriented HEA electrocatalysts to multi-element automotive alloy catalysts operating in exhaust environments, addressing degradation mechanisms specific to transient and low-temperature gasoline/hybrid-vehicle operation.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled post‐synthesis ammonia treatment to induce interstitial nitrogen doping in the multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst will form robust metal–nitrogen (M–N) bonds and promote a Pt‐rich surface layer, thereby mitigating activity loss and improving durability under transient, low‐temperature, H2O/NO‐rich exhaust conditions.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic ratios of principal elements, including platinum-group metals concentrated in a core–shell-like structure or randomly alloyed.
fields.intervention: Perform a controlled post‐synthesis ammonia treatment (thermal treatment under NH3 atmosphere) at a temperature optimized below significant sintering limits to incorporate interstitial N atoms.
fields.conditions: Transient and low-temperature exhaust operation conditions typical for gasoline/hybrid vehicles; exposure to H2O and NO; and thermal aging/mileage effects.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of multiple M–N bonds that pin the surface atoms, promote a slight tensile strain in the Pt-rich surface, and suppress leaching/dissolution of transition metals.
fields.mechanism: N-doping creates strong chemical bonds (M–N) between the dopant N atoms and non-noble metal constituents, thereby stabilizing the alloy structure and modifying the surface electronic structure (i.e., tuning the d-band center) to weaken adsorption of poisoning species. The induced tensile strain in the Pt-rich layer facilitates optimal reactant binding and accelerates turnover, similar to the beneficial effects observed in N–Pt/HEA/C electrocatalysts (see PMC10859931 records).
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, this intervention is predicted to reduce activity decay (e.g., lower voltage loss and mass activity drop) by approximately 20–30% under extended cycling, with enhanced resistance to oxidation and metal dissolution.
fields.baseline: The untreated catalyst suffers from moderate metal dissolution and agglomeration, leading to activity loss and durability issues under operating exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The benefits are expected under the regime of transient, low-temperature (e.g., <350 °C) exhaust operation with exposure to H2O and NO and under conditions simulating long-term thermal aging.
fields.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in activity and durability may vary depending on the precise N content and treatment temperature; uncertainties remain in scaling lab-scale treatment to full automotive conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical multi-element alloy catalysts.
